blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

Binary search halves the search space every step, giving **O(log n)**. It needs only one thing: a yes/no question whose answer flips exactly once as you move along the range. "Is `nums[i] >= target`?" flips from false to true in a sorted array. "Can Koko eat all the bananas at speed `k`?" flips from false to true as `k` grows. Find the flip point and you have the answer.

That second example is the idea that separates beginners from experienced candidates: you can binary search **on the answer**, not only on an array. Look for it whenever a problem asks for the *minimum value that is enough* or the *maximum value that still works* and checking one candidate is easy.
"sorted", "rotated", "minimum capacity or speed such that", "smallest value that satisfies", "in O(log n)".
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text:
| Variant | Question that flips | Typical problems |
|---|---|---|
| Find an exact value | `nums[mid] < target` | Binary Search, Search a 2D Matrix |
| Lower bound | first index with `nums[i] >= target` | Time Based Key-Value Store |
| Rotated array | which half is sorted | Find Minimum, Search in Rotated Sorted Array |
| On the answer | `canFinish(mid)` | Koko Eating Bananas |
| Partition two arrays | left half is no larger than right half | Median of Two Sorted Arrays |

Pick **one** template and learn it until the boundaries are automatic. The version below keeps the invariant "the answer is in `[lo, hi]`" and uses a half-open style that avoids the infinite loops of `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` mistakes.

blocks.title: BinarySearchTemplates.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** In `minEatingSpeed` the loop never touches an array being searched: it searches the range of possible speeds `[1, max pile]`, and the sorted-ness comes from the monotone question. The hours are summed in a `long` because a large pile count with a speed of 1 can exceed `int`.

`Arrays.binarySearch(array, key)` returns the index, or `-(insertionPoint) - 1` when the key is absent. `Collections.binarySearch` does the same for lists. Know it, but write the loop yourself in an interview.
blocks.title: The standard library already has it

blocks.text:
- **Overflow.** `(lo + hi) / 2` overflows for large indices; write `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.
- **Infinite loops.** With `lo < hi`, always move `lo` to `mid + 1` or `hi` to `mid`, never `lo` to `mid`.
- **Mixing two styles.** `while (lo <= hi)` with `hi = mid - 1` and `while (lo < hi)` with `hi = mid` are both correct but must not be mixed.
- **Wrong search space** on the answer: make sure the true answer lies inside `[lo, hi]` and that the question is monotone.
- **Duplicates** change which half is sorted in rotated arrays; that variant needs extra care.

The problem asks for the smallest or largest value satisfying a condition, checking one candidate value is easy (usually a linear scan), and the condition is monotone: if a value works, every larger value also works (or the reverse). Search the range of candidate values and use the check as the comparison.
blocks.title: Interview angle: How do you recognise "binary search on the answer"?
Key points
blocks.text:
- Binary search needs a yes/no question that flips exactly once
- Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` and one consistent loop style
- Lower bound is the building block for most variants
- You can search on the answer, not only on an array
- In a rotated array, one half around mid is always sorted
- Sum in `long` when the check can overflow `int`

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Binary Search** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: What is the time complexity of binary search and why?
items.answer: O(log n): each step discards half of the remaining range, so n elements need about log₂ n steps.

items.question: Why does `hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`) appear in the lower-bound loop?
items.answer: `mid` itself may be the first index that satisfies the condition, so it must stay inside the range. The loop ends when `lo == hi`, which is the answer.

items.question: Koko can eat at most 10 piles of up to 10⁹ bananas in 10⁹ hours. How many check iterations does the search need?
items.answer: About log₂(10⁹), roughly 30. Each check is a linear scan of the piles, so the total is O(n log maxPile).
